chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
title: A trip to New York with his drums, jamming and sitting in with Basie
summary: Lee took his drums on a bus to New York, met Freddie Green, Jo Jones, J.C. Heard and others, and sat in with Basie in Brooklyn.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And so I did that with George Estolle and them --and it did launch me as a -- it helped me immensely in the studios. But after that, I think, was when Lionel Hampton came back with Benny Goodman, when he broke up in 1940; he came out here and he formed his band, and what he wanted for the rhythm section was Nat's trio and myself, you know. And all the young musicians then just loved big bands, you know, because that's what it was, you know; Andy Kirk, Benny, and Artie Shaw, Charlie Barnet, you know --Basie and Lunceford-- and everybody on the west coast really loved big bands, and so Hampton just left Goodman, so when he come out -- he really wanted Nat, but I had been to New York on my own one summer -- I put my drums on a bus to go back there; I put my drums on a bus to go to New York to really see if I could make it with the guys.
Yeah. Yeah. And, this was when I met -- let's see, Tyree was living at Ms. Waters' apartment, you

know, Tyree Glenn, that is, and Don Byas was, but I went there and met Freddie Green, and that's -- at that time, Les Paul, I think it was -- Les? Yeah, I think it was Les ... he was big in radio in New York, I think. I'm sure it was Les Paul, because he would come to the jam sessions someplace down in Morningside; a place they used to go down under, almost underground, and that was the first time that I went there, and Jimmy Mundy was getting ready to form a band, also.

You know, Jimmy Mundy was going to form a band, and I stayed there -- and I would go to every -- I played all over New York, going in jamming. I remember, you know, you hear of all these drummers; you're from the West Coast, and they never did talk too much about West Coast musicians at the time, because they thought -- they had the reputation of being good readers, but they didn't think that West Coast musicians could improvise, or [tad taoud] (PHONETIC) as they called it, right?

These were drummers that I'm sure that everybody out east was aware of; thus, I met Kaiser Marshall who was a drummer, I met O'Neal Spencer, then I met Big Sid Heard, I met Joe Jones, I met J.C. Heard, I met Face, who was Zootie Singleton; and it was quite an experience, you know, to go from Los Angeles to New York.
Was Lester in New York when you were there?

Yeah, Lester was in New York, but it was funny -- I was going around with J.C. Heard, and Jo Jones. That's the three of us that was hanging out together, and we'd go to all these places and we would play. I think Basie -- when I was there at this time, Basie was playing at the Brooklyn Roseland, you know. And I got a chance to sit in on a couple of sets with him, then, you know, and that just blew me away!

Oh, yeah -- because it's unimaginable, really. So anyway, I put my drums back on the bus and came back and was -- on American Trailways, it was called -- a long trip across country with your drums on a bus. Well, I saved up my money, because I wanted to go and really find out. So ...
How long were you in New York?

Well, I think I stayed about 3 weeks until my money ran out. And then it seems to me that Lionel left Benny and he came back to the West Coast. Now before Lionel went with Benny, you mentioned the Paradise -- that's where Benny Goodman got Lionel Hampton; from the Paradise down on Main Street. It was between 6th and 7th on Main Street; a club called the Paradise, right? And Lionel Hampton had the band then, for a long time. And so did C.P. Johnson, later, and so did Charlie Echols.
